As of 140 PM EST Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1:  Unseasonably warm weather will continue across the 
region this afternoon, with high temperatures climbing into the 50s 
and lower 60s. A coastal low will gradually track northwards along 
the East Coast, with increasing cloud cover expected tonight and 
through the day tomorrow. Overnight lows will generally be in the 
30s to lower 40s with the increasing clouds, although some of the 
colder hollows may be able to radiate out earlier in the night under 
calm conditions. Rain chances look to arrive late Sunday into 
Monday, with the best chances for rainfall across southeastern 
Vermont. Compared to the previous forecast, rainfall amounts have 
decreased a bit, with generally 0.25 to 0.50 inches across eastern 
Vermont and the Upper Valley, with amounts sharply dropping off 
heading northwest across the forecast area. There continues to be 
some uncertainty amongst guidance in regards to the low track given 
the weaker nature of the low, but generally most guidance supports 
the lower rainfall amounts. A cold front looks to push through the 
region Monday night as the coastal low shifts eastward, which may 
drive some light terrain showers, although moisture looks to be 
limited.

KEY MESSAGE 2: In the wake of the departing coastal low and a sharp 
cold front, colder and blustery conditions are expected under 
northwesterly flow. High temperatures on Tuesday look to only climb 
into the 30s, nearly 20 to 25 degrees colder than the previous day. 
The brisk northwesterly flow will continue to make it feel quite 
blustery, with apparent temperatures in the 20s to low 30s on 
Tuesday, quite the drastic difference from the 50s and 60s this 
weekend. These colder conditions look to remain in place through mid-
week, with temperatures slow to moderate as strong ridging builds 
into the region. Under the influence of the building high pressure, 
dry conditions are expected for the start of next week, with no 
impactful weather currently expected Tuesday or Wednesday for any 
holiday travel plans.

KEY MESSAGE 3: After a mainly dry day on Wednesday, precipitation 
chances increase for Thanksgiving into the weekend with models still 
indicating some sort of coastal or double-barrel low pressure 
system. There remains considerable spread in solutions however, and 
expect it'll ultimately come up to fine details in temperature and 
moisture/wet bulb profiles. Airmass ahead of the incoming moisture 
plume will be quite dry (noted the 21/12z GFS has PWATs of 0.25 inch 
or less on Wed), lending toward evaporative cooling at the onset of 
the precipitation. As noted by the previous forecaster, the ridge in 
place is quite strong, and it will likely take a while for 
precipitation to make much northern/eastern headway. A strong S/SE 
jet will help keep temperatures aloft close to or above freezing 
until the low pulls away to our east and cold air advection starts, 
so it may very well depend on how quickly any colder air at the 
surface is able to be scoured out and/or warming is able to occur 
due to downsloping along northern/western slopes of the higher 
terrain. Probabilities of rain vs snow are somewhat equal, though 
tend to lean warmer/more rain for valley locations and cooler in the 
mountains. Freezing rain potential is harder to pin down, but note 
the latest NBM probabilities for freezing rain are 10% or less. This 
mostly makes sense as any freezing rain would likely occur at the 
snow-to-rain transition and would be brief and localized. However, 
our usual cold prone spots with a northeast wind (ie the northern St 
Lawrence Valley and far northwestern Champlain Valley of NY) could 
conceivably hold onto colder air longer, though surface temperatures 
will likely be close to freezing, either way. And all that's only 
applicable if we get any precipitation at all; several GEFS members 
give us little to nothing with just a glancing blow for our 
southeastern areas. Regardless, expect gusty winds Thursday and 
Friday given the strength of the jet (60+ kt around 850 mb), 
especially at summit level. We'll continue to watch trends closely 
as the Thanksgiving holiday approaches, and we urge you to do the 
same, especially if you have outdoor or travel plans.
